cards.title: Can a static dictionary be built deterministically in linear time?
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer d≥1 there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs A_d,Q_d and a constant C_d≥1 such that, for every n≥2, every word length ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉≤w≤d⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, A_d builds a static dictionary in at most C_d n operations and C_d n words of total space, and Q_d answers every membership-and-value query in at most C_d operations.
cards.context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records (12,5), (47,9) and (103,2) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of n² possible keys occupies n² cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic O(n log n) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general O(m(log log m)²) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to Θ(log m). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

cards.definitions: The universe is U_w={0,…,2ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs (x_i,v_i)∈U_w×U_w with pairwise distinct x_i and arbitrary v_i; the input order is unrestricted. On query q∈U_w the output is (1,v_i) if q=x_i and (0,0) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved w=Θ(log n) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

cards.title: Can all pairwise sums X+Y be sorted in quadratic time?
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer n≥2 and every X=(x₁,…,xₙ), Y=(y₁,…,yₙ)∈ℝⁿ, A outputs a permutation ((i₁,j₁),…,(i_{n²},j_{n²})) of [n]×[n] satisfying x_{i_r}+y_{j_r}≤x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}} for 1≤r<n², in at most Cn² unit-cost operations?
cards.context:
The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The 2017/2018 decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large groups of 50 and 24 small groups of 20: 980 planned places and 20 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. Top 100 and Top 1000 use the first 5/2 and 50/20 category places respectively. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
